content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable tempura is a Japanese dish consisting of bite‑size pieces of vegetables coated in a light batter made from flour, starch, egg and cold water, then deep‑fried. The result is a crisp, airy crust that keeps the natural flavor and tenderness of vegetables such as bell pepper, eggplant, broccoli, carrot and pumpkin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tempura was introduced to Japan in the 16th century by Portuguese missionaries.
The batter is kept cold, sometimes with ice, to create a light, airy coating.
Rice flour or corn starch is often added to the batter for extra crunch.
Vegetable tempura is commonly served with soy sauce, teriyaki, or a special tempura dipping sauce (tentsuyu).
In Japan, a “tempura‑zen” platter includes a variety of vegetables and seafood.

items.title: Rich source of vegetables
items.content: Tempura retains most of the vitamins and minerals of the original vegetables, such as vitamin C, beta‑carotene and potassium.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared correctly
items.content: When fried quickly in a small amount of oil, tempura remains relatively low‑calorie compared with other fried foods.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetables provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vitamins and phytochemicals in the vegetables help combat free radicals.

items.title: Natural glutamates
items.content: Some vegetables, like tomatoes and mushrooms, contain natural glutamate that enhances flavor without added MSG.

items.title: Seafood cross‑contamination
items.content: Even vegetable tempura is often fried in the same oil as seafood, which can be a problem for people with shellfish allergies.

items.title: Oil temperature
items.content: Maintaining the correct frying temperature (170‑180 °C) is essential; too low a temperature makes the batter absorb excess oil.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Dipping sauces are usually salty; those monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Potential foodborne hazards
items.content: Use fresh vegetables and clean oil to avoid bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tempura hot, typically with soy sauce, teriyaki, or tentsuyu. A light sprinkle of salt or toasted sesame seeds adds flavor. The crispy coating pairs well with a light broth or rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Tempura is best enjoyed immediately after frying. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 1‑2 days; reheat in the oven to restore crispness.
